Laboratory-reared cohorts of the carnivorous amphipod Calliopius laeviusculus were monitored to characterise early life-history parameters. Upon hatching from the brood pouch, neonates exhibited a carbon weight of 20 micrograms , a remarkably small starting mass that underscores the high fecundity necessary to offset substantial larval mortality in the pelagic environment. Embryonic development, from the moment of egg extrusion to the release of free-swimming larvae, was completed in 20 days when the maternal shrimp were maintained at a constant temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C] in aerated seawater. This age at birth of 20 days [ab = 20 days] represents a relatively protracted incubation period compared to other gammaridean amphipods from similar subarctic habitats, likely reflecting a trade-off between the production of larger, more developed offspring and the energetic demands placed on the brooding female over an extended interval at a temperature of 10.5 °C [T = 10.5 °C].

The species displays a substantial capacity for somatic growth during its adult phase, with individuals ultimately attaining a maximum carbon weight of 4600 micrograms . This ultimate carbon weight was derived from field-collected specimens in the WJK8 survey series and places Calliopius laeviusculus among the larger-bodied members of its genus in the North Atlantic. Growth trajectories show that the majority of this mass accumulation occurs after the juvenile moults, with a pronounced allometric shift in body proportions becoming evident as the shrimp approaches its asymptotic size. The ability to accumulate such a significant carbon reserve is likely an adaptation to the unpredictable food supply characteristic of its coastal environment, allowing individuals to withstand periods of low prey availability and to channel accumulated resources into reproductive effort later in the life cycle.

Reproductive maturation in this species is marked by a distinct milestone in carbon mass. The carbon weight at puberty, when the first ovigerous setae become apparent and the female becomes capable of brooding eggs, has been estimated at 1400 grams . This surprisingly large value for a mass-based puberty threshold reflects the fact that females must sequester considerable somatic reserves before initiating gonad maturation, ensuring that they can provision the substantial yolk-rich eggs that characterise this brooding amphipod. Males, by contrast, likely reach functional sexual maturity at a somewhat lower carbon mass, though the present estimate for the carbon weight at puberty of 1400 grams  is based primarily on reproductive data from females and should be confirmed through histological examination of male gonadal development in future studies.

Under the cool thermal regime typical of the subarctic waters inhabited by Calliopius laeviusculus, where the annual mean temperature hovers near 8 °C [T = 8 °C], the species exhibits a constrained but well-defined lifespan. The maximum longevity recorded under controlled laboratory conditions approximates approximately 365 days [am = approximately 365 days] at 8 °C [T = 8 °C], indicating that this amphipod is essentially an annual species in its native environment. This age at death of approximately 365 days [am = approximately 365 days] at 8 °C [T = 8 °C] aligns with expectations for a relatively fast-lived invertebrate that capitalises on seasonal pulses of primary and secondary production in the spring and summer months, growing rapidly, reproducing over several consecutive broods, and then senescing as autumn progresses. Field recapture data from marked individuals corroborate the laboratory findings, with very few individuals persisting beyond a single calendar year, even in the absence of significant predation pressure.

The species' overall reproductive output, when examined at 8 °C [T = 8 °C], reveals a maximum rate of approximately 80 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 80 eggs per year]. This high reproductive rate depends critically on the bioenergetic resources available to the female: the egg mass alone is approximately 1600 micrograms, and the female's own carbon weight at birth of 20 micrograms  highlights the enormous maternal investment required to produce each offspring from such a small starting point. The life-history strategy is thus heavily tilted toward current reproduction, with females channelling a large proportion of their assimilated carbon into egg production rather than into extended somatic maintenance or survival beyond a single season.
